newsitem.title: USA: U.S. arrest of Spanish businessman causes concern.
newsitem.headline: U.S. arrest of Spanish businessman causes concern.

text.p: His family and lawyer call Francisco Javier Ferreiro-Parga a legitimate merchant who does business with Cuba. The U.S. government says he trades with the enemy.

Ferreiro, a 45-year-old Spaniard, was arrested on April 11 on charges that he breached the U.S. economic embargo against the communist-ruled island by shipping containers full of canned food, diapers and sanitary napkins from Miami to Cuba.

The arrest of a foreign businessman, and his subsequent indictment by a federal grand jury on charges of contravening the U.S. Trading With The Enemy Act, has stirred a wave of concern among foreigners trading with Cuba.

It has also raised speculation the United States has stepped up enforcement of the 35-year-old embargo, its major, oft-maligned weapon in the fight launched by the late U.S. President John Kennedy to dislodge President Fidel Castro's government.

The indictment of Ferreiro, who is now in a federal detention centre in Miami, could also raise the hackles of European nations at a time when they are pressing the United States to moderate Helms-Burton, the controversial law that seeks to punish foreigners trading with Cuba, experts said.

"This signals a step up. Enforcement has been stepped up," said Max Castro, a senior research associate at the University of Miami's North-South Centre. "It didn't just happen. The guy wasn't caught red-handed. The U.S. had to go looking for him."

In the past, Trading With The Enemy violators have been caught randomly by the Coast Guard or Customs bringing small quantities of Cuban cigars or rum to the United States. In one recent case, a Philadelphia businessman allegedly smuggled nearly 1,300 Cuban cigars bought during a boat trip to Cuba.
But enforcement of the act against commercial enterprises has been sporadic, with perhaps one or two cases a year and none in some years, U.S. authorities said.

Prosecutors have accused Ferreiro of setting up a series of dummy corporations to funnel consumer goods through third countries to Cuba, where the government distributed them to hotels and tourist shops to feed a demand for U.S. products.
"The magnitude of it is unusual," Customs agent Keith Prager said. "It's rare that you get a criminal enforcement."

While the hardline Miami Cuban exile community is rabidly anti-Castro and abhors contact with Cuba, federal agents said trade with the communist-run island is a cottage industry in Miami -- at least some of it conducted by exiles. In the 1970s and 80s, it was easy to find bottled Coca-Cola and U.S.-made cigarettes there, officials said.
"It's always been here. It never shrunk," Prager said. "It started to grow the day in 1962 when Kennedy said he would embargo Cuba."
Customs official deny that there was any political motivation behind the Ferreiro indictment, saying it resulted from routine investigation.

While it would be difficult to prove a political motive, analysts said, the Ferreiro case could be aimed at appeasing a hardline anti-Castro faction in Congress to win concessions for moderating Helms-Burton, which in turn would appease European allies.
"Maybe it's being prosecuted now because of the different political climate in the U.S.," said Andrew Zimbalist, an economist and Cuba expert at Smith College in Massachusetts.
Yet at the very least, the indictment has highlighted the divergent attitudes toward Cuba, with the United States trying to isolate Castro, and Europe and Canada taking a more conciliatory tack.
Ferreiro's indictment also is a source of concern for Spanish businesses trading with Cuba and has led to speculation that the U.S. might be taking aim at legitimate businessmen.
